Abstract 14

Graphene oxide (GO) efficiently enhances macroscale mechanical properties of cement-based 15

materials. Yet the nanoscale reinforcing mechanism of GO for calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H), 16

the key binding phase of concrete, remains poorly understood. Moreover, how polycarboxylate 17

ether (PCE)-based superplasticizers affect the nanomechanical properties of C-S-H remains 18

unclear. The intrinsic mechanical properties of the nanocomposites are measured using high- 19

pressure X-ray diffraction. The influences of GO and PCE on the local Ca and Si environments 20

are probed using X-ray absorption spectroscopy. For the first time, we evidence that PCE- 21

induced well-dispersed GO nanoplatelets strengthen the C-S-H basal planes, whereas poorly 22

water-dispersed GO weakly interacts with basal planes and does not strengthen in plane Ca-O 23

bonds. Both PCE and GO only slightly strengthen C-S-H’s c-axis. The bulk modulus of C-S- 24

H/PCE/GO nanocomposite is 190% than pure C-S-H. Functional groups of PCE and GO prefer 25

interacting with the Ca-O sheets of C-S-Hs instead of silicate tetrahedra. 26

27

Keywords: C-S-H; PCE; GO; nanocomposite; bulk modulus. 28

1.Introduction 30

Nanomaterials are common additives for modifying the mechanical properties, durability, and 31

rheology of cement-based materials [1]. The addition of nanomaterials, including but not limited 32

to calcium silicate hydrate (C−S−H) seeds, nanosilica, nanoclay, and carbon nanotubes, in 33

cement-based materials have been extensively studied [2] [3]. Graphene and graphene oxide 34

(GO) are among the hottest topics in materials science due to their supreme properties, e.g., large 35

surface area (1500+ m2/g) with two-dimensional morphology and high intrinsic in-plane 36

Young’s modulus (380-470 GPa for GO) at the nanoscale (defect-free level) [4] [5]. Note that 37

the microscale modulus of GO can be just tens of GPa due to the defects between planes in 38

aggregated GO [6]. Their use is trendy in scientific research of cement-based materials and 39

alkali-activated materials [7] [8] [9]. Recent advances in research and development of graphene 40

and GO manufactures results in scalable production and lower cost, making their use in concrete 41

practical [10] [11] [12]. 42

43

Graphene is a single atomic layer of graphite, consisting of sp2 bonded carbon atoms arranged in 44

a hexagonal lattice [13] [14]. GO is the oxidized form of graphene with functional groups (e.g., 45

carbonyl, epoxy, hydroxyl, and carboxyl) [15]. The GO incorporation in binder matrixes is more 46

favorable relative to the graphene incorporation due to the stronger interactions between cement 47

pastes and GO functional groups [16]. The addition of GO in cement-based materials results in 48

improved tensile and compressive strengths due to a refined microstructure of pastes [17] [18] 49

[19]. The strength improvement is more pronounced when GO nanoplatelets are dispersed by 50

superplasticizers, typically polycarboxylate ether (PCE)-based [20]. A nanoindentation study has 51

showed that the addition of GO does not enhance the microscale Young’s modulus of C-S-H (the 52


<!-- Page 5 -->


3

primary binding phase of concrete) [21]. In contradiction, molecular dynamics simulations have 53

indicated GO-strengthened C-S-Hs at the nanoscale [22]. There remains a gap between 54

understanding the micro- and nano-scale influences of GO on the C-S-H mechanical properties. 55

The nanoscale mechanical properties of C-S-H in the presence of GO need to be experimentally 56

validated. Measuring the nanomechanical properties of GO-incorporated C-S-H is important, yet 57

challenging. Additionally, the influences of comb-shaped PCE (a hotly studied and widely used 58

superplasticizer) on the nanomechanical properties of C-S-Hs are still poorly understood. 59

60

High-pressure X-ray diffraction (HP-XRD) is a powerful tool to determine the intrinsic 61

mechanical properties of (nano)crystalline phases [23] [24] [25]. In HP-XRD experiments, the 62

microstructure influences (e.g., mesopores and crystal size) on nanomechanical properties 63

measurement can be eliminated by filling pressure-transmitting medium into the mesopores. 64

Thus, hydrostatic pressures can be applied onto C-S-H nanocrystallites, and their 65

nanomechanical properties can be measured at the scale of unit cells. HP-XRD has been 66

successfully applied to determine the influences of Ca-to-Si molar ratio (Ca/Si) [26], Al 67

incorporation [27], cross-linking structures [28], synthesis method [29], and decalcification [30] 68

on the intrinsic mechanical properties of nanocrystalline C-S-Hs. 69

70

In this study, a pure nanocrystalline C-S-H reference and C-S-H-based nanocomposites with the 71

additions of GO and PCE are synthesized. The influences of GO and PCE additions on the 72

coordination environment of Ca and Si of C-S-H are studied using X-ray absorption near-edge 73

fine structure (XANES) spectroscopy. The intrinsic mechanical properties of C-S-H and 74

PCE/GO incorporated C-S-H nanocomposites are investigated using HP-XRD. The 75

nanomechanical properties of the nanocomposites are correlated to their nanostructure, and the 76

PCE-GO synergic effect is evidenced. The GO reinforcing mechanism of nanocrystalline C-S-Hs 77

is unveiled. The results have great potential in optimizing GO incorporated cement-based or 78

alkali-activated materials for buildings, oil-cementing, and carbon storage capping when 79

inexpensive GO is largely available. Our results are also valuable for validating nanoscale 80

simulation of binary and ternary systems of C-S-H, PCE, and GO, as well as providing the first- 81

hand data to develop forcefields of molecular dynamics for understanding C-S-H’s interaction 82

with polymers and GO. 83

2.Materials and methods 85

2.1 Materials and synthesis 86

Pure C−S−H (the reference group) was synthesized at an initial Ca/Si of 1.0 using the co- 87

precipitation method [29]. Stoichiometric amounts of Na2SiO3·9H2O (99+%, Fisher) and 88

Ca(NO3)2·4H2O (99+%, Fisher) were separately dissolved in 250mL deionized water in two 500 89

mL HDPE bottles in a N2-filled glovebox at 25 °C. The water to solid precursors (Na2SiO3·9H2O 90

and Ca(NO3)2·4H2O) mass ratio was 50. Na2SiO3 solution was continuously dropped into 91

Ca(NO3)2 solution, immediately forming a white slurry. The initial pH of the suspension in the 92

pure C−S−H system was 12.03. The sealed bottles were shaken at 60 rpm for seven days at 93

25 °C. Subsequently, the slurry was filtered using 0.45 μm nylon membranes with a vacuum 94

pump (flow rate 37 L/min, Millipore Sigma) under N2 protection. The remnant gel-like product 95

was vacuum-dried for seven days at 25 °C with the presence of 10 g NaOH pellets (97+%, 96

Fisher) in a 10.5 L glass desiccator to minimize carbonation. 97

98

C−S−H-based nanocomposites, C−S−H/GO, C−S−H/PCE, and C−S−H/PCE/GO, were 99

synthesized also using the co-precipitation method, but with the addition of GO, PCE, and a 100

PCE-GO mixture, respectively. GO was synthesized using the modified Hummers method [31]. 101

A comb-shaped PCE with a molecular weight of 36000 g/mol [32] was used in this study. The 102

number of side chains (molecular weight 1000 g/mol) in one molecule is 27. The carboxylate to 103

ether ratio is 2.67. The number of ethylene oxide monomers in one side chain is 23. For C-S- 104

H/PCE synthesis, the PCE solution (30 wt.%) was dropped into a 250mL Ca(NO3)2 solution. The 105

rest of mixing protocol of C-S-H/PCE system followed the C-S-H synthesis. Before curing for 106

seven days, the system pH was adjusted to 12.03 by dropping 174 μL of 1N NaOH solution 107

(FisherSci). 108

109

The GO used in this study has been characterized earlier in [33]. No additional phase was found 110

in this batch. Our GO contains 10% of carboxyl and 15% of carbonyl groups on the plane edges. 111

The core region of GO with an O/C molar ratio of 0.23 contains 60% hydroxyl and 40% epoxy 112

groups. The intrinsic (nanoscale) Young’s modulus of GO depends on the degree of oxidation 113

[4]. For the used GO with O/C=0.23 in our experimental study of nanomechanical properties of 114

C-S-H nanocomposites, its Young’s modulus is 410 GPa. The GO aqueous solution (15 mg/mL) 115

was ultra-sonicated for 10 min before the nanocomposite synthesis. The mixing protocol of 116

nanocomposites considerably impacts their dispersion and further properties [34]. GO 117

immediately agglomerated in the Na2SiO3 solution in our trial mix because GO hardly stabilizes 118

in highly alkaline environments, consistent with existing literature [34]. Thus, for the synthesis 119

of C-S-H/GO, GO solution was added into Ca(NO3)2 solution, followed by 10 min ultra- 120

sonication. Na2SiO3 solution was then dropped into GO-Ca(NO3)2 solution, followed by pH 121

2.2 X-ray absorption near-edge fine structure spectroscopy 135

The XANES spectra of the C−S−H and C−S−H-based nanocomposites at the Ca L2,3-edge were 136

collected using the scanning transmission X-ray microscopy at the bend beamline 5.3.2.2 of the 137

Advanced Light Source (ALS) at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The energy step 138

of each scan is 0.1 eV. The experimental setup is detailed in [36]. The XANES spectra at the Si 139

K-edge were collected at the PHOENIX beamline of the Swiss Light Source at Paul Scherrer 140

Institute, Switzerland. The data were collected using a fluorescence-yield mode with a 500 μm × 141

500 μm beam at room temperature. The spectra were recorded at an energy step of 0.15 eV for 1 142

s for each data point. More experimental details can be found in [37]. 143

2.3 High-pressure X-ray diffraction 145

The HP-XRD experiment was conducted at the superbend beamline 12.2.2 of the ALS. A BX90 146

diamond anvil cell was used for pressurizing the samples. A 250 μm thick rhenium gasket was 147

pre-indented to ~100 μm thick by the diamond anvil pair. A 110 μm diameter cylindrical 148

chamber was laser-milled at the indent center. Each powder sample was loaded into the chamber, 149

followed by the blending with 1-3 ruby microspheres [23]. The chamber was filled with 150

pressure-transmitting medium (ethanol-methanol solution at 1:4 volume ratio) before an 151

immediate closure with the diamond anvil pair. The applied hydrostatic pressure to the sample 152

was determined by an offline fluorescence station. The size of the X-ray beam (wavelength 153

0.4959 Å) was ~30 μm x 30 μm. Diffraction patterns at elevated hydrostatic pressure and at 154

ambient pressure were collected from the chamber and sample-filled silica capillaries, 155

respectively. The diffraction peaks were fitted using Marquardt fitting method with PVII type in 156

XFIT [38]. Celref [39] was used to refine the B11m tobermorite structure [40] in the pressure 157

range of 0 – ~10 GPa. 158

3.Results and discussion 170

3.1 Ca and Si coordination environments 171

*Fig.1A shows the XANES spectra of the C-S-H and C-S-H-based composites at the Ca L2,3-edge. 172*

The spectra result from the electron transition from 2p to 3d orbitals of Ca [41]. Two major 173

peaks, a2 and b2, originate from the loss of degeneracy of 2p orbitals (2p3/2 and 2p1/2) by spin- 174

orbit coupling. Minor peaks (a1 and b1) are observed at the left of each major peak due to crystal 175

field splitting [42]. The leading peak a0 corresponds to the mixing of states due to the 3d spin- 176

orbit splitting effect and multipole interactions of core holes with valence electrons. The b2 peaks 177

of C-S-H/GO and C-S-H/PCE are positioned at 0.05 eV lower energy compared to the b2 peak of 178

C-S-H. The a2 and b2 peak energies are 0.1 eV and 0.03 eV, respectively, lower than those of C- 179

S-H/GO and C-S-H/PCE. Note that the a2 and b2 peak energies of C-S-Hs are very sensitive to 180

Ca-O coordination and typically vary in a short range, within 0.1 eV [36]. Thus, the a2 and b2 181

peak shift of C-S-H nanocomposites, although not noticeable, can be an index for the variation in 182

coordination environment (e.g., coordination number of Ca) of C-S-H-based materials. The 183

energy shift suggests that the addition of PCE and/or GO induces a smaller mean coordination 184

number of Ca [29], i.e., more CaO sheets are six-fold coordinated in the C-S-H-based 185

nanocomposites compared to the well-accepted CaO7 sheet in C-S-H. 186

Si K-edge XANES spectra of the C-S-H and C-S-H-based composites are shown in Fig.1B. The 213

major peak B (Si K-edge) at ~1839.8 eV is attributed to the dipole-allowed transition of 1s 214

electrons to 3p orbital of Si [48]. The post-edge humps D at ~1847. 5 eV and E in an energy 215

range of 1845-1855 eV correspond to the multiple-scattering effect from more distant 216

coordination shells and the 1s-3d electron transition of Si, respectively. The Si K-edge energy is 217

very sensitive to the silicate polymerization degree of tobermorite-like phases (e.g., C-S-H) [36] 218

[37]. The variation in Si K-edge energy of C-S-H with various degrees of silicate polymerization 219

is 1.5 eV. Thus, the low variation (<0.12 eV) of Si K-edge energy among our four C-S-H and 220

nanocomposite samples suggests a comparable degree of silicate polymerization and poor 221

interaction between the additives and C-S-H silica tetrahedron. The addition of PCE and/or GO 222

exhibits negligible influences on the silicate mean chain length because 1) the additives prefer 223

interacting with CaO sheets; and 2) the interactions between the silicate tetrahedra and GO epoxy 224

and hydroxyl groups are more favorable in the presence of bridging Ca [8]. The poor interaction 225

between the additives and silicate tetrahedra can be explained by the lack of bridging 226

functionality (e.g., silyl groups) of the additives [46]. 227

4.Conclusions 301

This study presents synchrotron radiation-based material characterizations of nanocrystalline C- 302

S-H and PCE- and/or GO-modified C-S-H nanocomposites. The intrinsic mechanical 303

(nanomechanical) properties of the C-S-H-based samples at the unit cell level are measured. The 304

key conclusions are: 305

• The intralayer Ca of C-S-H weakly interacts with the functional groups in the presence of 306

only PCE or GO. The interactions between intralayer Ca and GO are strong in the 307

presence of a PCE-GO mixture. CaO sheets are more six-fold coordinated and less 308

distorted in the C-S-H/PCE/GO nanocomposite. 309

• PCE, GO, and the PCE-GO mixture all prefer interactions with Ca rather than Si. Neither 310

PCE nor GO exhibits pronounced influences on the coordination environment of Si of the 311


<!-- Page 17 -->


15

nanocomposites. The influences of the functional groups on the lattice parameters of all 312

samples are relatively low. 313

• In the presence of only PCE or GO, the basal planes of C-S-H are not reinforced, while 314

only the c-axis is slightly strengthened. The bulk moduli of C-S-H/PCE and C-S-H/GO 315

increase by up to 24% compared to the pure C-S-H reference. 316

• In the presence of the PCE-GO mixture, the basal planes are significantly stiffer, while 317

the c-axis is only slightly strengthened. The bulk modulus of C-S-H/PCE/GO is 90% 318

higher than that of the C-S-H reference due to the PCE-GO synergic effect. PCE- 319

dispersed GO nanoplatelets significantly reinforce C-S-H basal planes. 320

321

The results provide the first experimental evidence for the reinforcement of C-S-H with PCE-GO 322

at the nanoscale. This study provides new insight into the reinforcing mechanism of PCE-GO for 323

C-S-H building blocks and the nanostructure of C-S-H-based nanocomposites. Therefore, this 324

work has great implications in designing GO-reinforced cement-based or alkali-activated 325

materials in service. 326
